contents.text: Similes and metaphors are figures of speech that compare two things that are not actually alike.

header.text: A simile compares two things by saying that one is like the other. Similes often use the word like or as.

sentences.text: My sister runs like a cheetah.
The sister's running and a cheetah's running are compared using the word like.
A cheetah is known for running fast, so the simile means that the sister also runs fast.
The cat's fur was as dark as the night.
The cat's fur and the night are compared using the word as.
The night is dark, so the simile means that the cat's fur is also dark.

header.text: A metaphor compares two things by saying that one of them is the other. Unlike similes, metaphors don't use the word like or as.

sentences.text: The snow formed a blanket over the town.
The snow and a blanket are compared without the word like or as.
A blanket is a large piece of cloth that completely covers a bed. The metaphor makes the reader imagine that the snow becomes a blanket, covering the town completely.

contents.text: Using similes and metaphors in your writing can help you create an interesting picture for the reader.

textContent.text: Marilyn sighed and pulled out her phone as soon as she sat down. She had just learned the repairs to her car would cost twice as much as she expected. The waiting room chairs were stiff, and the TV blared a commercial about vacations she couldn't afford.
She opened a game on her phone, trying to block out everything around her. The longer she played, the heavier her mood felt.

Out of the corner of her eye, she noticed a little girl twirling in a sparkly dress dotted with shimmering circles. The girl's mother stood at the counter, talking to a mechanic, her face tight with worry.
"Hi!" the girl said brightly, tapping Marilyn's arm. "I'm Lila."
"Hello," Marilyn replied, not looking up from her screen.
"This is my mermaid dress!" Lila announced proudly, spinning so her skirt glittered.
"Nice," Marilyn murmured, still focused on her game.
For a moment, Lila was quiet. Marilyn noticed her stop twirling and stand still, watching. Then, to Marilyn's surprise, the child sat down beside her and folded her hands in her lap.
The silence between them was soft and surprising.

After a moment, Marilyn sighed and turned off her phone. For the first time that morning, she really noticed the sunlight on the floor tiles, the hum of the air, and the kind little girl beside her. It was oddly peaceful.
"Rough morning," Marilyn said quietly.
Lila nodded. Then she peeled one of the shiny stickers from her skirt and placed it in Marilyn's palm. "A mermaid scale," Lila whispered. "It makes sad days better."
Marilyn smiled for the first time all day. "Thank you," she said.
Lila grinned and pulled out a coloring book. "Want to color with me?" Marilyn leaned forward and smiled. She was surprised at how much lighter the room felt.

<atomic>"Hello," Marilyn replied, not looking up from her screen.</atomic>
<atomic>"This is my mermaid dress!" Lila announced proudly, spinning so her skirt glittered.</atomic>

textContent.text: Maya's heart raced as she stood at the pool's edge. Her lifeguard certification test was just moments away. Although she'd spent weeks perfecting her strokes and building endurance, she was now a bundle of nerves. The pool she'd practiced in at least a hundred times suddenly felt like the ocean. She adjusted her goggles, trying to focus, but doubt crept in.

Jamal looked over and noticed Maya's nervous expression. "Hey Maya," he said, offering a warm smile. "You've got this. I saw you practicing last week, and you're really strong!" His words were simple but sincere, and Maya stood up tall. She nodded gratefully and took a deep breath.

The whistle blew. Maya dove in, her strokes cutting through the water just as she had practiced. The 300-yard distance was tough, but she heard Jamal's words echo in her mind and she pushed through. Next came the rescue drill. When the head lifeguard blew his whistle, she jumped in, swam to the deep end, and sank to grab a brick off the bottom. Her lungs burned, but she surfaced and carried the brick to the edge of the pool. The final task—treading water with her feet while holding a weight overhead—was difficult, but Maya knew she could do it. She only had to last two minutes, and she had practiced the task for as long as five minutes every day that week.

Exhausted but smiling from ear to ear, Maya climbed out of the pool. "You passed!" said the head lifeguard, giving Maya a pat on the shoulder. As she dried off, she grinned at Jamal, who gave her a thumbs-up.

Sophia began to worry as she saw five more hands shoot up, each one held up to suggest a different idea. She kept a running list of the group's suggestions, realizing that choosing just one design would disappoint many people. Still, she promised to consider all of their ideas.
After school, Sophia lingered so she could talk to Mrs. Dannon, the student council's advisor.

textContent.text: Tumble was a shy gnome who spent his days exploring, mostly so he could be alone. He had never enjoyed the attention of others—not that anyone ever paid him much attention. The quietest one of the group, Tumble was constantly ignored by the other gnomes in the forest.

One morning, as Tumble climbed high into the hills, he heard some voices in the distance. Not wanting to be seen, he dashed into a small, hidden cave. But something caught his eye. In the back corner, resting on a pile of moss, glowed a silver egg, humming softly.
Tumble's eyes widened. "A dragon egg!" he whispered. Familiar with the legends, he knew he must find the mother before it hatched, or it wouldn't live.

Tumble tucked the egg under his arm and scurried out of the cave, toward Dragon's Peak. The thought of going near the massive dragons made his knees tremble. He stopped for a moment and looked at the egg. "If I don't help this little creature, no one will," he whispered. And with that, he kept going.

pieces.text: Nearing Dragon's Peak, Tumble felt the lump in his throat getting bigger.

content.text: What will I say? Will the dragons believe I am trying to help the egg?

pieces.text: He set the egg down and looked at it. The egg gave a little shake, and Tumble remembered that there was a little baby in there. He forced his feet forward, and soon he was face-to-face with a large red dragon.

textContent.text: Tumble gulped as he held the egg toward her. "It was all alone. I wanted to make sure it would be okay." The dragon sniffed the egg and smiled.
"You've done well, brave gnome. Others would have left it," she said. The dragon offered Tumble a ruby as thanks, but he shook his head.
"Knowing the egg is safe is enough," Tumble explained.
As he made his way back home, Tumble stood taller. For the first time, he was looking forward to telling others what he had done.

textContent.text: Snow blanketed Greenfield Road, and school was closed. Thirteen-year-old Whitney and her friends, Zoe and Grayson, bundled up in scarves and mittens and began to shovel the wet snow into a pile. With bright eyes and lots of laughter, they shaped an igloo in Whitney's front yard, its rounded roof glistening under the winter sun. Grayson steadied the walls while Zoe packed the snow tighter, and Whitney brushed off the loose edges. The three of them paused now and then to laugh at their crooked spots before fixing them together. With their project completed, they went inside to prepare a thermos of hot chocolate. Then they returned to enjoy the warm cocoa in their new, wintry fort.

Across the street, Whitney noticed Mr. Thompson, their quiet neighbor, peering out his window. He lived alone, his children having gone off to college and other adventures years ago. Whitney's heart tugged as she thought of how kind he'd been to her over the years. "Let's invite Mr. Thompson," she said, surprising her friends. The three trudged to his door, snow crunching under their boots, and invited him to visit their igloo and sample the hot chocolate they had made.

Mr. Thompson, bundled in a long, thick coat, shuffled over with a shy smile. Inside the igloo, the kids shared stories of school friends and favorite sledding hills. Mr. Thompson told them about winters when his children had enjoyed similar adventures. The kids listened with wide eyes as Mr. Thompson began his story. "Once," he said, "a blizzard blew in and covered the town for a whole week! My son and his friends decided to put on a snowman contest. I still remember trying to fit a superhero costume on a very large, round snowman." The igloo filled with laughter.

As dusk painted the sky pink, Mr. Thompson thanked them, his voice thick with emotion. "I haven't had a day like this in years," he said. Whitney and Grayson smiled, and Zoe patted Mr. Thompson's arm. "We are really glad you came over," said Whitney. "Maybe next time we can try to make a super-snowman, too!"

<atomic>With bright eyes and lots of laughter, they shaped an igloo in Whitney's front yard, its rounded roof glistening under the winter sun. Grayson steadied the walls while Zoe packed the snow tighter, and Whitney brushed off the loose edges. The three of them paused now and then to laugh at their crooked spots before fixing them together.</atomic>
<atomic>With their project completed, they went inside to prepare a thermos of hot chocolate. Then they returned to enjoy the warm cocoa in their new, wintry fort.</atomic>

<atomic>Across the street, Whitney noticed Mr. Thompson, their quiet neighbor, peering out his window. He lived alone, his children having gone off to college and other adventures years ago. Whitney's heart tugged as she thought of how kind he'd been to her over the years. "Let's invite Mr. Thompson," she said, surprising her friends.</atomic>
<atomic>The three trudged to his door, snow crunching under their boots, and invited him to visit their igloo and sample the hot chocolate they had made.</atomic>
<atomic>Mr. Thompson, bundled in a long, thick coat, shuffled over with a shy smile. Inside the igloo, the kids shared stories of school friends and favorite sledding hills.</atomic>
<atomic>Mr. Thompson told them about winters when his children had enjoyed similar adventures. The kids listened with wide eyes as Mr. Thompson began his story.</atomic>

<atomic>"Once," he said, "a blizzard blew and covered the town for a whole week! My son and his friends decided to put on a snowman contest. I still remember trying to fit a superhero costume on a very large, round snowman." The igloo filled with laughter.</atomic>
<atomic>As dusk painted the sky pink, Mr. Thompson thanked them, his voice thick with emotion. "I haven't had a day like this in years," he said.</atomic>
<atomic>Whitney and Grayson smiled, and Zoe patted Mr. Thompson's arm. "We are really glad you came over," said Whitney. "Maybe next time we can try to make a super-snowman, too!"</atomic>

textContent.text: Jeremy finished tying his cleats, then jogged to the center of the field for stretches. Joining the huddle, he was surprised to find a man he didn't recognize talking to the team.
"I'm Coach Ned," the man said with a grin. "I'm excited to be your new coach!"

Practice was different right from the start. Coach Ned set up a series of cones, and the players had to dribble around them while singing goofy songs. Soon, everyone was giggling. As they practiced, Coach Ned ran up and down the sidelines, cheering and complimenting their skills. He seemed to be having just as much fun as they were.

After a week of practices filled with laughter and energy, it was finally time for their first game. At halftime, they were losing 5–0. Coach Ned gathered the team together as the players slumped onto the grass, sweaty and frustrated.
"What's the point?" one of them muttered. "We're just going to lose." Jeremy nodded, feeling the same way. For the first time, he wanted to give up.
"Listen up!" Coach Ned said with his usual smile. "I want you to answer this question: Why do you play soccer?"

The team was quiet. Finally, Jeremy spoke. "Because it's fun," he said softly. Others agreed. They shouted that they liked being with friends, feeling the wind while they ran, and laughing with teammates.
"Funny, no one said they played to win games," Coach Ned said. He looked around, watching his words sink in. "For the second half of the game, play for the reasons you just mentioned."

Jeremy ran out onto the field, excited to start the second half. He played better than he ever had. The team ended up losing 5–4, but they high-fived after every goal, helped each other up when they fell, and felt a new team energy they had never experienced before. More importantly, they couldn't wait for their next game.

textContent.text: Liam grinned at his friends' lunchtime stories as he reached for his roll. Pulling it apart, he noticed it was warm and soft—unlike the hard rolls the cafeteria usually served. He took a bite and was amazed by its buttery flavor. Looking around the table, it seemed that his friends were having a similar experience.
Liam grabbed his fork and dove into his mashed potatoes, then the chicken. He couldn't believe it—this food was amazing!
Liam could see how excited and confused his friends were. This could make a great story for the school newspaper! Quickly, Liam grabbed his notebook and walked over to the lunch line.
Behind the lunch counter, he noticed a man dancing and singing as he placed another tray of dinner rolls into the oven. When the man whirled around, he noticed Liam and turned down the radio.
"What can I do for you, young man?" he asked kindly.
"I just wanted to ask about the food." Liam explained, pencil in hand. When he noticed the man's worried expression, he quickly added, "No, it's amazing! Did you make it?"
The man's smile lit up his entire face as he nodded. The chef moved quickly around the kitchen, humming as he stirred and chopped. Liam could tell he loved what he was doing.
"Do you think I could write about you for the school paper?" Liam asked. "Everyone will want to know who you are!"
The man looked at Liam thoughtfully, then laughed out loud. "I guess that would be all right. I always wanted to be famous!" he said with a wink.
"How did you get into cooking?" Liam asked.
The man paused, then smiled. "I've always seen food as art. It's what led me to become a chef."
The chef told Liam about working in a famous kitchen and why he now cooked at a school. Liam scribbled notes as fast as he could in his notebook. This was going to be an amazing story!

textContent.text: Marilyn sighed and pulled out her phone as soon as she sat down. She had just learned the repairs to her car would cost twice as much as she expected. The waiting room chairs were stiff, and the TV blared a commercial about vacations she couldn't afford.
She opened a game on her phone, trying to block out everything around her. The longer she played, the heavier her mood felt.

Out of the corner of her eye, she noticed a little girl twirling in a sparkly dress dotted with shimmering circles. The girl's mother stood at the counter, talking to a mechanic, her face tight with worry.
"Hi!" the girl said brightly, tapping Marilyn's arm. "I'm Lila."
"Hello," Marilyn replied, not looking up from her screen.
"This is my mermaid dress!" Lila announced proudly, spinning so her skirt glittered.
"Nice," Marilyn murmured, still focused on her game.
For a moment, Lila was quiet. Marilyn noticed her stop twirling and stand still, watching. Then, to Marilyn's surprise, the child sat down beside her and folded her hands in her lap.
The silence between them was soft and surprising.

After a moment, Marilyn sighed and turned off her phone. For the first time that morning, she really noticed the sunlight on the floor tiles, the hum of the air, and the kind little girl beside her. It was oddly peaceful.
"Rough morning," Marilyn said quietly.
Lila nodded. Then she peeled one of the shiny stickers from her skirt and placed it in Marilyn's palm. "A mermaid scale," Lila whispered. "It makes sad days better."
Marilyn smiled for the first time all day. "Thank you," she said.
Lila grinned and pulled out a coloring book. "Want to color with me?" Marilyn leaned forward and smiled. She was surprised at how much lighter the room felt.

contents.text: A plural noun names more than one person, place, or thing.
A possessive noun shows who or what owns something or has something.

header.text: Add an apostrophe and -s ('s) to a singular noun to make it a possessive noun.

contents.text: Matt → Matt's glove
the bird → the bird's wings

header.text: When a plural noun ends in -s, just add an apostrophe (') to make it a possessive noun.

contents.text: the boys → the boys' camp
the schools → the schools' teams

header.text: When a plural noun does not end in -s, add an apostrophe and -s ('s) to make it a possessive noun.

contents.text: the children → the children's toys
the mice → the mice's tails
